title: Linux Cron and Job Scheduling
description: Schedule recurring and one-time tasks using crontab, at, and systemd timers for automated system maintenance.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with cron installed, your ordinary account user is allowed to use crontab and already has scheduled entries. Use crontab to list your own entries.
tasks.explanation: crontab -l displays the invoking account's scheduled entries. Running sudo crontab -l would select root instead; your own crontab needs no elevation.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with cron installed, your ordinary account user is allowed to use crontab. Neither VISUAL nor EDITOR is set, and the default editor is available. Use crontab to open your own entries for editing.
tasks.explanation: crontab -e opens your entries in the selected editor and installs the changes when editing finishes. VISUAL and EDITOR can select the editor; with both unset, Ubuntu uses the default editor. This edits your account's crontab without sudo.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with cron installed, your ordinary account user is allowed to use crontab and has an existing crontab. Use crontab to remove your entire crontab without a confirmation prompt.
tasks.explanation: crontab -r removes every entry in your crontab without prompting; it does not remove another account's crontab or system-wide cron files. sudo without -u would act on root's crontab instead.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with cron installed, backup has a crontab. Your ordinary account user has sudo access. Use crontab with elevation to list backup's entries.
tasks.hint: Use crontab with user flag (-u): 'sudo crontab -l -u backup'
tasks.explanation: -l lists entries and -u backup selects backup's crontab. sudo permits inspecting another account's crontab. Omitting -u after sudo would instead list root's crontab.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, at is installed, atd is running, and your account user is allowed to submit jobs. It is before 14:30 local time today. /home/user/backup-job.sh is readable and contains complete /bin/sh commands using absolute paths. Use at to submit that file's commands as your one-time job for 14:30 today, without interactive input.
tasks.hint: Read the existing job file with -f: 'at -f /home/user/backup-job.sh 14:30 today'
tasks.explanation: at -f reads job commands from a file instead of its interactive prompt and queues them for /bin/sh under your account. atd executes the queued job later. Since 14:30 is still ahead, omitting today also selects today. sudo would submit as root rather than as user.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, at and atq are installed, and your ordinary account user is permitted to use them. Use atq (or at's listing option) to list all of your pending one-time jobs.
tasks.hint: Use atq to list pending jobs: 'atq'
tasks.explanation: atq and at -l show pending jobs owned by the invoking account. Running atq as root would show everyone's jobs, so sudo does not match this request.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, the system manager has active and inactive timers but no failed timer units. As an ordinary user, use systemctl to list the active system timers and their next run times when available, without including inactive timers.
tasks.explanation: list-timers queries the system manager by default and shows timer schedules, including NEXT and the service each timer activates. --all also includes inactive timers and does not fit this request. Reading timers needs no elevation; --user would inspect a different manager.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, anacron is installed and has recorded the cron.daily job's last run date in /var/spool/anacron/cron.daily. This file and its parent directories are readable by your account. Use cat to display that recorded date.
tasks.hint: Use cat to view the file: 'cat /var/spool/anacron/cron.daily'
tasks.explanation: Anacron records a job's last execution date in its spool file and uses that date to decide whether it is due. cat reads this existing date; it neither runs the job nor updates its timestamp. The stated read permissions make sudo unnecessary.
